title: Declassified Air Force Files Document Four 1950s UFO Sightings Over Santa Catalina Island

content:
Four declassified Air Force intelligence reports spanning 1949 to 1955 document separate observations of unidentified objects in the vicinity of Santa Catalina Island, the Channel Islands landmass roughly 29 miles off the coast of Southern California. The observers range from a family who wrote directly to Kenneth Arnold – the pilot whose 1947 sighting coined the term “flying saucers” – to Boy Scouts on a mountain hike and an Air Force sergeant scanning the night sky from the mainland. The reports were filed through four different channels, assessed with four different conclusions, and are now all classified as unresolved.

The reports are designated DOW-UAP-D177, DOW-UAP-D178 and DOW-UAP-D179 and were published as part of the seventh release under the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE). Each carries the declassification authority NND 923007.

1949: a letter to Kenneth Arnold

The earliest of the four reports did not enter the Air Force’s intelligence system through official channels. It arrived as a handwritten letter addressed to the man most closely associated with the phenomenon itself.

On 1 May 1949, Percy E. Wachey of PO Box P-1, Avalon, Catalina Island, wrote to Kenneth Arnold at his home in Boise, Idaho. Arnold’s sighting of nine objects near Mount Rainier on 24 June 1947 had made him the most recognised civilian witness in the country and had given the English language the phrase “flying saucer.” By 1949, Arnold had received thousands of letters from members of the public reporting similar observations.

Wachey’s letter, written three days after his sighting, reads:

“About 8 o’clock of the night of April 28th, my wife and a school teacher saw six objects in the sky, not in a group, but singly. A few minutes later after going to my daughter’s home, on the next street and corresponding block, she and my daughter and my grandson saw four more. All traveling in the same direction.”

The letter closes: “If you are still interested in flying disks, saucers etc., please let me know and I will write more in full.”

Wachey helpfully added at the bottom: “Avalon is on Catalina Island, about 25 miles from Long Beach, Calif.”

The letter reached the Air Force. A routing card shows it arrived at the 17th District office at Kirtland Field, New Mexico, on 20 May 1949 and was forwarded to IAXS – the intelligence analysis section at Air Materiel Command headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, the same facility that administered the Air Force’s successive UFO investigation programmes. It was recorded there on 26 May 1949 at 1100 hours, assigned control number Q-1216, and filed under the subject heading “Unknown Aerial Phenomena.”

A marginal notation on the letter reads: “MCIAXS did not acknowledge this ltr.”

The Air Force never wrote back.

The sighting occurred during the brief tenure of Project Grudge, the Air Force’s second UFO investigation programme, which had succeeded Project Sign in February 1949 and would itself be wound down by December of that year. Grudge’s final report, published in August 1949, concluded that UFO sightings could be attributed to conventional objects, mass hysteria and hoaxes.

The Project Blue Book record card for the case – filed retroactively when Blue Book consolidated earlier records – lists six objects, a civilian source, ground-visual observation, and no photos or physical evidence. The course, length of observation and time group are all recorded as “not reported.” The conclusion reads: “INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR EVALUATION.”

The PURSUE programme has classified the report as unresolved.

1952: three Boy Scouts at Camp Fox

Three years later, another sighting from the island reached the Air Force, this time through the formal reporting system.

Three Boy Scouts at Camp Fox summer camp on Santa Catalina Island observed an object during a mountain hike on 25 June 1952. The report, prepared by Lieutenant Colonel E.D.H. Maddox of the 807th Air Base Group at March Air Force Base, describes a silver object at an uncertain altitude. Its speed was “estimated to be faster than a conventional jet.” No sound was observed.

One manoeuvre was recorded: the object apparently made a climbing turn immediately before disappearing. The report’s language for the manner of disappearance is “disintegration.”

The sighting occurred at noon under clear, unlimited sky conditions. The length of observation was not recorded. No observing instruments were available.

The report includes four enclosures: letters from the three scouts – Clyde Vrooman, Howard Howell and Sam Gates – and a fourth letter from Forrest E. Spriggs dated 1 July 1952. Two of the enclosures contained rough sketches of what the observers saw.

The report was filed under AF Letter 200-5, the predecessor directive to Air Force Regulation 200-2 that governed the reporting of unidentified flying objects. It was not submitted until 28 August 1952 – two months after the sighting. Maddox noted that “no report has been made by electrical means due to the time lag in the receipt of the information at this installation.”

The report’s evaluation field reads: “None.” The reporting officer offered no reliability assessment of the observers, noting that “the experience of the observers is probably meager at best.”

Copies were distributed to Strategic Air Command, the Fifteenth Air Force, and the Chief of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.

March Air Force Base was a Strategic Air Command installation in Riverside County, approximately 60 miles east of Los Angeles. In 1952 it was home to the 22d Bombardment Wing, which operated B-29 Superfortress bombers and was beginning to receive KC-97 aerial refuelling tankers. The Boy Scouts’ sighting reached the Air Force’s intelligence system through one of SAC’s bomber bases.

1953: an Air Force sergeant watches from San Pedro

The third report records a ten-minute observation by a military witness on the night of 16 November 1953.

Technical Sergeant Robert J. Currie, aged 39, was at the intersection of Tenth Street and Gaffey Street in San Pedro, the port district of Los Angeles that faces directly across the San Pedro Channel toward Catalina Island. His home address is listed as PO Box 294, San Pedro, with a secondary address at 720 Harbor Hill, Lomita. His occupation was Air Force clerk.

Currie reported one round, saucer-shaped object. It appeared purplish white on first sighting and faded to white before disappearing. He estimated its apparent size as that of a pea.

The object appeared stationary during the initial sighting, positioned over Catalina Island at 45 degrees elevation. It then moved northwest toward Los Angeles on a straight, level horizontal path before fading from view. No erratic manoeuvres were observed. The total observation time was ten minutes.

The report was filed by the 2347th Air Force Reserve Training Center at Long Beach Municipal Airport and transmitted by teletype to Air Defense Command at Ent Air Force Base in Colorado Springs, the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson, the Director of Intelligence at USAF headquarters in Washington, and Continental Air Command at Mitchel Air Force Base in New York.

Weather conditions were clear, with ten miles visibility. Winds aloft ran northwest at 8,000 feet, shifting through 250 to 280 degrees at altitudes from 10,000 to 28,000 feet.

The report notes that the movement of the object “does not coincide with winds aloft.” Astronomers at Griffith Park Observatory were consulted and “aver at objects such as these are possibly planets which appear more clearly after rain fall.” The report records Jupiter’s position on 15 November as 5 hours 38 minutes, at 45 degrees elevation in the west.

Currie was assessed as “fairly reliable due to association with jet aircraft activity while stationed at Long Beach Air Force Base.”

The Project Blue Book summary card records the conclusion as “Astronomical (JUPITER).” The PURSUE programme has classified the report as unresolved.

1955: a bright object falls over Avalon

The fourth report documents a two-second observation over Avalon, the small harbour town on the eastern shore of Catalina Island, on the night of 15 March 1955.

The observer, Paul J. Carr of 222 Descanso Street, Avalon, reported one round object approximately the size of a nickel held at arm’s length. It was very bright and orange in colour. It changed from orange to red, then fell straight down before fading from sight. The total duration of observation was approximately two seconds.

The report was filed under AFR 200-2 by the 670th Aircraft Control and Warning Squadron, a radar unit assigned to the air defence of the Southern California coast. The teletype originated from San Pedro and was routed to the 27th Air Division (Defense) at Norton Air Force Base, Air Defense Command at Ent, the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson, and the Director of Intelligence at USAF headquarters.

Weather conditions were clear, dry and cool. Visibility was unlimited.

Captain Clifford E. Brant, USAF Intelligence Officer, assessed the report. His conclusion: “Flight path and length of time in sight, suggest UFOB was probably a meteor.”

The 4602d Air Intelligence Service Squadron – the field investigation unit attached to Project Blue Book, with detachments across the United States trained in counterintelligence and rapid-response assessment – reviewed the case. Its assessment was recorded as “possibly astronomical, but due to the brevity of the sighting, no further investigation was deemed worthwhile by this organization.”

The Project Blue Book record card marks the conclusion as “Was Astronomical – Meteor.” A separate UFOB Index Card for the same incident records the conclusion as “Probably Astronomical.” The intelligence officer’s own assessment used “probably.” The 4602d AISS used “possibly.”

The PURSUE programme has classified the report as unresolved.

The reporting chain

The four reports followed different paths into the Air Force’s intelligence system, but each arrived at Wright-Patterson.

The 1949 report bypassed the system entirely. A civilian wrote to Kenneth Arnold in Idaho; the letter was routed through the 17th District at Kirtland Field in New Mexico and filed at Air Materiel Command headquarters at Wright-Patterson. No one wrote back.

The 1952 report was filed by March Air Force Base, a Strategic Air Command bomber installation 60 miles inland. The 1953 report was filed by the 2347th Air Force Reserve Training Center at Long Beach. The 1955 report was filed by the 670th Aircraft Control and Warning Squadron, a radar unit whose mission was air surveillance over the Pacific approaches to Los Angeles.

The three later reports were all forwarded to the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson, which administered Project Blue Book, and to the Director of Intelligence at USAF headquarters in Washington. The 1953 and 1955 reports were also routed to Air Defense Command headquarters at Ent Air Force Base.

Santa Catalina Island sits within the line of sight of the air defence radar stations that guarded the Southern California coast during the Cold War. The 670th ACWRON, which filed the 1955 report, operated from San Clemente Island Air Force Station between 1952 and 1961, maintaining radar coverage of the Pacific sector that included the waters around Catalina. It later moved to Fort MacArthur and manned the radar installation on San Pedro Hill, overlooking the same channel from the mainland side.

What the documents show

The four reports span three different Air Force investigation programmes. The 1949 letter was filed during Project Grudge, the short-lived successor to Project Sign that concluded UFO sightings were attributable to conventional explanations, mass hysteria and hoaxes. The 1952 case was filed during the early months of Project Blue Book. The 1953 and 1955 cases were assessed by Blue Book’s mature apparatus, including consultation with Griffith Park Observatory astronomers and the 4602d AISS field investigation unit.

Across six years, four sets of observers – a family on an island who wrote to the most famous civilian UFO witness in the country, three Boy Scouts on a summer camp hike, an Air Force sergeant stationed at Long Beach, and a civilian resident of Avalon – reported objects in the same patch of sky. The reports accumulated four different institutional responses: no acknowledgement, no evaluation, an astronomical identification the report’s own data questioned and an explanation that three different assessors expressed in three different degrees of certainty.

The graduating language of the assessments is itself a feature of the record. The 1949 report received no reply. The 1952 report was given no evaluation. The 1953 report received a definitive conclusion – “Astronomical (JUPITER)” – despite the reporting officer’s own note that the object’s movement did not match the winds and despite the Griffith Park Observatory astronomers’ qualification of their assessment as “possibly” planetary. The 1955 report accumulated three words on a single card: “was,” “probably” and “possibly” astronomical, from three different assessors reviewing the same two-second observation.

Percy Wachey’s 1949 letter to Kenneth Arnold asked whether Arnold was “still interested in flying disks, saucers etc.” and offered to “write more in full.” The marginal notation on the letter – “MCIAXS did not acknowledge this ltr” – suggests the full account was never requested.

The PURSUE programme has classified all three as unresolved. They are now among the 478 records available through the PURSUE programme. Chief Pentagon Spokesman, Sean Parnell, confirmed the Department of War and its agency partners “are actively working on the next release of UAP files” and that material will continue to be published “on a rolling basis.” No timetable has been announced for the eighth release.

Last Updated on October 28, 2026 by Nick Ross
